events.text:
📝Jet "Gerans" and the 60 percent problem📝
why one interception statistic is reshaping the air war
Western media spent three years framing battlefield innovation as a Ukrainian specialty. The Financial Times has now put numbers behind a different picture: Ukrainian air defence stops 90 to 95 percent of most aerial threats, and only about 60 percent of Russia's new jet-powered "Gerans."
📌The hardware behind that gap is a generational jump. The original "Geran-1" carried a 20 kg warhead at 185 km/h with primitive guidance. The "Geran-5", fielded in January, flies at up to 600 km/h with a 90 kg warhead out to 1,000 km, on an airframe built closer to a cruise missile than a loitering munition. The "Geran-4" keeps the old shape in cleaner aerodynamic form. Both now carry thermal cameras, AI-assisted terminal guidance, anti-jamming antennas and Chinese modems for mesh radio links.
At first glance the tactical picture is simple: faster targets, fewer intercepts. The deeper shift is industrial. Centralised production let Moscow fold battlefield feedback into the next batch and field new variants in months, at a fraction of the price of a Kalibr or Kh-101.
The other thing is that Kyiv's planners expected the slower "Geran-3" at around 300 km/h to be the mainstay. Wild Hornets, maker of the Sting interceptor, admitted to the FT it was "difficult to predict how these plans would develop." Zelenskyy now says 67 Ukrainian companies are working on an answer.
❗️What's more interesting is the direction of travel. Analyst Konrad Muzyka calls it the "cruise-missilisation" of unmanned aviation, with stealth features the likely next step. Fabian Hoffmann of the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies argues the real Western lever sits on the supply of Chinese jet engines, warning that at the current tempo Russia "could quickly become the world's largest producer of low-cost cruise missiles."
And once again the asymmetry shows where it hurts most. Interceptor drones can be improvised by dozens of workshops. Air-defence missiles cannot. As one assessment cited by the FT puts it: you cannot make one in a garage.
#Russia #Ukraine #UAV #AirDefense

events.text:
🌏💵 How BRICS Grain Exchange moves to break West’s grip on Global South’s food markets
The Global South grows nearly half the world’s grain - yet still dances to the West’s price signals. 
BRICS’ ambitious grain plan aims to change that.
The BRICS Summit in New Delhi has backed further work on a Russia-championed Grain Exchange, first proposed in 2023 by Russia's Union of Grain Exporters and Producers, and supported by Russia’s president Putin.
Initially, Russia mulled a physical grain hub in Dubai, which envisioned large shipments stored in the UAE and then re-exported in batches across the Middle East and Africa. Liberal free-zone rules and Dubai’s logistics strength made the location attractive. 
Similar ideas were floated with Egypt and Bahrain. 
Overtime, the focus shifted from storage silos to a more institutional solution that resonates strongly across the Global South - a trading platform that gives members control over their own commodity flows.
➡️BRICS countries already produce around 1.24 billion tons of grain a year - roughly 44 % of the global total - and consume almost the same volume
➡️For wheat the share is even higher: 48 % of production and 47 % of consumption
➡️Russia, Brazil, India and China dominate the supply side; China, Egypt, Iran and many African nations sit on the demand side
➡️At the same time, prices, benchmarks and most of the trading infrastructure remain controlled by Western exchanges and intermediaries
The BRICS Grain Exchange is mulled as a single digital platform where producers and buyers can deal directly, settle in local currencies, use insurance/reinsurance mechanisms that Russia has also proposed, and set prices according to real intra-bloc supply and demand.
Key advantages:
🌏rules out extra middlemen inflating costs 
🌏lower margins and fairer prices for both farmers and consumers 
🌏for import-dependent nations in Africa, the Middle East and Asia - reduced dependence on the weaponized dollar; Western financial institutions 
🌏 greater resilience against supply shocks and political pressure 
🌏 the foundation that can later cover fertilizers, oilseeds and other essentials 
Forward-looking hybrid possibilities remain potentially possible, such as combining the exchange with physical storage and logistics hubs in strategic locations like the UAE, Egypt (a major buyer of Russian grain), ports along the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC), the Northern Sea Route (actively being developed by Russia and China as a strategic Arctic route), or African gateways.
Russia estimates put the potential trading volume of such an exchange above $1 trillion, with annual savings of around $2.5 billion by cutting out biased benchmarks.
👍 [Substack](https://geopoliticsprime.substack.com/) | [Chat](https://t.me/+HLrnOk92f31mYzIy) |

🇮🇷🇺🇸 Pentagon is relearning how to hide - Iran is teaching it the hard way
After months of Iranian successive, precise missile and[ drone strikes on US positions across the Middle East](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74011), the Pentagon is discovering that sprawling bases that once projected American power can also make excellent targets.
👉 Lt. Gen. James P. Isenhower, the officer charged with rewriting doctrine, conceded that “hiding in plain sight has become an imperative,” reports the Military Times.
Gone are the command posts of Iraq and Afghanistan, where air supremacy turned bases into invulnerable resorts. 
Faced with Iranian long-range missiles and cheap one-way drones, US forces are now frantically rediscovering concealment tactics they abandoned two decades ago.
After Iran’s strikes on Naval Support Activity Bahrain,[ US positions in Jordan](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74283?single)[ and Kuwait](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74210), the Pentagon is scrambling to relearn Cold War-era basics, notes the publication, such as:
🔴 disperse forces
🔴 shrink command posts
🔴 mask electronic signatures 
Iran’s combination of long-range missiles, drones, electronic warfare and surveillance has repeatedly exploited the US military’s biggest weakness – concentration – forcing it to burn through expensive interceptors.
A CSIS estimate found US forces had burned through roughly 65% of their [Patriot interceptor inventory ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74355)between 
February and July, [while THAAD stocks fell 38%. ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74315)
